newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean prosecutors sift evidence on Kim's son.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean prosecutors sift evidence on Kim's son.

text.p: South Korean prosecutors said on Saturday they were sifting through a mountain of papers seized in a probe into rumours that President Kim Young-sam's son took a 200 billion won ($226 million) kickback.
The documents were confiscated in a police raid on Friday on the home and offices of a businessman, identified by local media as an associate of the president's second son, Kim Hyun-chul.

Prosecutors are probing rumours that Hyun-chul took 200 billion won from the businessman acting as an agent for failed Hanbo Steel Co. An opposition politician, who first levelled the charges, has said the money took the form of a rebate on imported German machinery.
Hyun-chul is now at the centre of a parliamentary probe into the collapse of the steelmaker in a bribery and influence-peddling scandal.
Ten people, including a former cabinet minister and close political aides to president Kim, are on trial for their roles in the scandal.
"As the volume of documents is huge, it will take a time to go through them," said a prosecution official.
Police hauled away boxes of papers and computer floppy discs from the property of businessman Park Tae-joong.
The official also said prosecutors were probing 11 accounts at 10 banks held by Park and his relatives.
Hanbo Steel became South Korea's biggest corporate casualty in January when it collapsed under $5.8 billion of debts.

Separately, prosecutors extended their probe into a doctor whose videotape of Hyun-chul discussing a top media appointment in his surgery has fuelled a political storm over the younger Kim's alleged meddling in state affairs.
A Seoul court on Saturday issued a warrant to search the home and offices of the doctor, Park Kyung-shik, a court official said.
Yonhap Television News said police later raided the premises in search of more videotapes, memos and diaries.
Parliament on Friday kicked off an investigation into funding for Hanbo and will call Kim Hyun-chul to testify.
The ruling New Korea Party agreed to the inquiry after opposition parties attacked an earlier probe by prosecutors as a whitewash that failed to expose leading players.

Kim Hyun-chul issued an apology on Monday for causing trouble and anxiety and said he was ready to accept punishment if he had done wrong. His father said on television last month he felt shamed his son had been linked to the Hanbo scandal.
The younger Kim has no official posts but is dubbed by newspapers the "crown prince".

"Even though more than two months have passsed since the Hanbo scandal broke, rumours and suspicions have never died. We are deeply concerned," ruling party spokesman Lee Yoon-sung said in a statement on Saturday.
"We believe revealing the truth is the only way to solve public suspicions."
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics welcomed an announcement on Friday that the chief prosecution investigator into the Hanbo affair had been replaced.

"The most important thing is for prosecutors to do something to recover public credibitily. Prosecutors have to re-probe the Hanbo scandal thoroughly from the beginning with a new investigation team," a party statement said.
"Kim Young-sam's regime is not a civilian government but a joint regime of Kim Young-sam and Kim Hyun-chul," it said.
